Hey Michael,

Just wanted to touch base with you on why some of the fields are not being populated into the MedicaidInquiry table. I have attached the spreadsheet where it shows the CarrierName through CoverageEnd doesn't have any data. Is this process supposed to be filling in those fields?

My Response:
Hey Jake, good question.

Most of those fields are left over from the first iteration of this process. At some point we should go in and drop CoverageType, CarrierCode, CoverageEffective, and CoverageEnd (or maybe we should actually be using the effective and end, not sure!)

CarrierName should have some values. Status DONE + no CarrierName means we completed the search but didn’t get a match. If there’s a Medicaid ID, you know we got a response from TennCare.

I’m a little surprised we don’t have any with CarrierName so far, but I guess it’s possible.

For what it's worth, those get mapped in two steps. When we’re reading in the HTML response from TennCare:
BLUECARE -> BLUECARE
TENNCARE SELECT -> TENNCARE SELECT
Starts with WELLPOINT -> WELLPOINT
Starts with UNITEDHEALTHCARE -> UHC TENNCARE

Those are the values you should see in the MedicaidInquiry table.

When we’re creating the insurance assignments, we derive the insurance ID from the carrier name as:
TENNCARE SELECT -> 1
UHC TENNCARE -> 2
WELLPOINT -> 3
BLUECARE -> 7
[null] -> 10


So it could be that we just haven’t hit any eligible students yet. Or we could be mapping something wrong. Might be worth watching the automation flow as it does its thing to see if there are some valid matches that aren’t making it through for some reason. That HTML request and response were really hard to mock accurately, so there could very well still be some glitches with the way we’re processing that page.

Would it be helpful to be thinking of a time for me to come out there and finish the server migrations, apply and troubleshoot the clock reader fixes, and apply and start doing the quarterly updates? I think we could probably make three good days out of that stuff, or at least two. Or if it’s better to do it as a series of Teams meetings, I can do that, too.

---

He responded with a friendly "thanks" but nothing else.

In the interim, I've been working on some background work on TTDS. I sent this Q4 update at the end of December:

---

Good afternoon, hope you're doing OK. I wanted to share a summary of my ongoing TTDS improvements for Q4 2025.

To review, Q3 focused on:
- usability and stability improvements (work order search performance, asynchronous processing improvements)
- code quality and maintainability (null handling, data processing performance, observability)
- modernization (C# 12 upgrade)

For Q4, since it seems like TTDS upgrades and migrations might be taking a back seat to other priorities right now, I decided to shift gears from the development work I had planned to do and to focus instead on future-proofing around the edges. Specifically, I've been working on (1) support and recovery documentation and (2) automated functional testing.

The support and recovery documentation is in a new TTDS "service repository" that I've created on GitHub. My focus has been primarily on:
- what would a new support person or developer need to know about TTDS to be able to work on it?
- what information would we want to have readily at hand in the event of a disaster, especially one requiring recovery of part or all of the system?
- what information might not be accessible to Tex Tech if I were for any reason not personally available?

I've completed most of the documents I set out to create. There are still a few stubs out there. I'll revisit those as time permits. Please suggest any revisions, clarifications, or additions that you think might be helpful.

Automated functional testing involves creating test scripts using a browser-automation and test-running tool called Playwright. These tests are in a separate testing repository. So far, I've created tests that will:
- log onto TTDS using test credentials
- create a work order using the UI
- create a work order and related items programmatically, trigger MRB creation by submitting a failing observation, and then verify that the MRB has been created as expected
- select an MRB disposition and verify that the UI updates as expected

Future tests might include:
- creating an inspection session and inputting data
- inputting lab test results
- working with more detailed MRB functionality
- testing the emissions-related features

I'm describing these tests as "future-proofing" work for a couple of reasons. One is that they document the intended behavior of the system in a way that's (a) maintained with the code and (b) readily consumable by developers. The other reason is regression: with these tests in place, we can be more confident that unrelated changes to TTDS don't break or destabilize these core features that we're testing.

To be clear, my only motive for thinking in terms of future-proofing is to be a responsible and reliable service provider. I'm not planning on going anywhere anytime soon.

For Q1, I'm thinking it might be valuable to:
- continue work on automated functional testing
- begin work on adding unit tests directly in the code
- explore ways to make the telemetry we added in Q3 more useful for direct TTDS monitoring

Of course, I'd be grateful for your feedback on how I'm using this time and whether you're finding it valuable.

---

I worked on this for a few hours this afternoon, and thought I had it figured out, but I kept running into foreign key problems. 

Thinking about it some more, I finally realized what the problem was.

I knew about the split increment problem, where the work order for the master roll might be archivable but not the work order for the finish roll, or vice-versa.

But there's another problem. Both roll scraps and graded defects are tied to inspection sessions. I had to do that in order to attribute those elements to specific inspectors for reporting.
And increments are also tied to inspection sessions. So you can have a situation where a roll scrap or graded defect isn't fully archivable, because it's tied to a session that has an increment tied to it that's not fully archivable.

That's a solvable problem for sure, but I don't think it's worth it. I've decided on a different approach:

1. Select all work orders that are archivable based on the date.
2. Archive those work orders and **all** related entities, whether they're fully archivable or not
3. Rather than delete based on the process-related "permanent temp" tables, delete based on what's in the archive table, but _only_ if there are no unarchived dependent objects

Consequences:

- Some work orders will take longer to be fully archived, but in all likelihood it'll just be another quarter
- Some work orders will be archived twice, in two separate batches; they could potentially be different; the later archive will be "the truth"

I'll rework the proc on my next work day and then test it out again using my local TTDSTest and TTDSArchive databases

summary.S: Revised approach for archiving work orders and related entities

# Migration Notes

This is meant to be a running note where I update the results of each migration.

## Abandon
The abandon page is just a way of abandoning the session.
I don't see where we ever call it.
I think we could probably safely remove it, but a little more research is needed.

## AddStudent
This is called from a button on the home page.
It works fine.
But it's probably worth finding out whether adding students is normally done in hub instead.
Suggestions for improvement:
- calendar control for DOB is not super useful since you have to click back month by month to get to a reasonable DOB for a school-age child (at least 60 clicks)
- validation message "Save Failed" isn't super helpful
- unless we use this form to add many students at a time, it would be better to close the form and maybe do a toast notification that it succeeded

## Attendance
This is a fairly complex page, and as far as I can tell, it's only called in a very specific circumstance, which may never happen.
From `CalTherapy.ascx`, on initial page load, it runs `usp_sel_EVENTDETAIL`,
which is a very weird stored proc that actually does a `UNION` and returns two rows (sometimes at least) for the same event.
But we're only reading the first row.
And only in cases where the `EV_ATTENDANCE_STATUS` is null, then we redirect from `CalTherapy.ascx` to `Attendance.aspx`.
But that doesn't make sense either, because `Attendance.aspx` isn't really a full page, it's clearly meant to run within the iframe,
but maybe that's where that redirect happens (I'm a little confused on that point).
My gut is that we never use Attendance.aspx anymore, only CalAttendance.aspx.
But I haven't been able to prove that.
There are a few stored procs that I had to add to test to get this page to work.
They may not actually be needed anymore:
- `usp_parmsel_ATTENDANCE_ByEventD` (sic)
- `usp_sel_ABSENT_REASON`
- `usp_sel_TREATMENT_CODES`
- `usp_parmsel_STUDENTS_BySchoolID`
- `usp_upd_EVENT_ByEventID`
- `usp_parmsel_CheckBeginAssessment` (this one uses an `exec` in production; I rewrote it in test)

Also, when it is called, it sets two query string parameters: `&EV_ATTENDANCE_STATUS=False&VerifyAttendance=True`, which aren't used for anything.


## GlobalErrorPage
This is called from `Global.asax` as the last-resort handler for errors other than `HttpException`

content.S:
This is my response to Holly's initial proposal:

I don’t see any reason we shouldn’t be able to almost completely automate the therapy orders. The basic process would consist of:

A monthly job that would create therapist referral records in Stellar Docs based on the criteria you outlined and then use DocuSign to create and send the envelopes
Some kind of process for monitoring the responses, which would then update Stellar Docs with the results
A way of handling non-responses
A way of flagging therapists not to send to again
A way of generating and sending the “heads-up” email

Pulling the data is detailed but seems straightforward enough. 

For generating the documents, we can get by without Doc Creator. If practical, the simplest option would be to set up a template in DocuSign. If that won’t work, we could write C# code to create the PDFs directly from the data (there are good free PDF libraries).

Monitoring can be either “pull" or “push". Pull would be a (daily?) batch job that would use the DocuSign API to check for responses. Push would be an endpoint we set up for DocuSign to send responses to. That could be either an API that we set up for that purpose (which could be really really useful for the admin changes and other things) or it could be something like an AWS lambda that drops a message in a queue that we could monitor via the StellarAutomationSupport service we implemented as part of the eligibility verifications. Either way, we would take the response and then update Stellar Docs based on the results.

Non-responses and flagging therapists could probably be part of the monthly job, actually. Just need a little more detail on exactly how that works.

Generating the heads-up email could be done automatically. Not sure if you guys already have an email service that you use, but there are a number of options. Or we could generate a report and somebody could send those manually if preferred.

This would require you to pay for the DocuSign API. Not sure how big of an expense that would be relative to what you’re paying now.

I’m not quite at a point where I’m ready to provide an estimate. I need to take a little time to dig into the reports you’re pulling to understand the data. Also, could you please tell me a little more about how importing the results works (step 12 in your instructions)? And if you could send me the form template(s), that would also be really helpful.

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT
    TC.ATT_STUDENT_ID,
    MostFrequentTherapist.Therapist_ID AS Supervisor_Therapist_ID,
    TC.IEP_IEP_ID,
    TC.REF_ID,
    TC.REF_SERVICE_ID,
    TC.SVA_services_Id,
    TC.IEP_Service_Type,
    TC.DIS_DISTRICTS_ID,
    TC.DIS_Name,

    --TC.SCH_Name,
    TC.IEP_BeginningDate,
    TC.IEP_EndingDate
into #SupervisorData
FROM #TherapistCred TC
CROSS APPLY (
    -- Subquery to find the most frequent therapist
    SELECT TOP 1 
        CASE 
            WHEN TC2.ESO_SIGNER_ID IS NOT NULL AND TC2.ESO_DISC_ID IN (13, 5, 8, 49) THEN TC2.ESO_SIGNER_ID
            WHEN TC2.ATT_Supervisor_ID IS NOT NULL AND TC2.ATT_DISC_ID IN (13, 5, 8, 49) THEN TC2.ATT_Supervisor_ID
            WHEN TC2.EV_THERAPIST_ID IS NOT NULL AND TC2.THER_DISC_ID IN (13, 5, 8, 49) THEN TC2.EV_THERAPIST_ID
            ELSE NULL
        END AS Therapist_ID
    FROM #TherapistCred TC2
    WHERE TC2.ATT_STUDENT_ID = TC.ATT_STUDENT_ID
      AND TC2.THER_SER = TC.THER_SER
      AND TC2.IEP_IEP_ID = TC.IEP_IEP_ID
      AND (
          (TC2.ESO_SIGNER_ID IS NOT NULL AND TC2.ESO_DISC_ID IN (13, 5, 8, 49))
          OR (TC2.ATT_Supervisor_ID IS NOT NULL AND TC2.ATT_DISC_ID IN (13, 5, 8, 49))
          OR (TC2.EV_THERAPIST_ID IS NOT NULL AND TC2.THER_DISC_ID IN (13, 5, 8, 49))
      )
    GROUP BY 
        CASE 
            WHEN TC2.ESO_SIGNER_ID IS NOT NULL AND TC2.ESO_DISC_ID IN (13, 5, 8, 49) THEN TC2.ESO_SIGNER_ID
            WHEN TC2.ATT_Supervisor_ID IS NOT NULL AND TC2.ATT_DISC_ID IN (13, 5, 8, 49) THEN TC2.ATT_Supervisor_ID
            WHEN TC2.EV_THERAPIST_ID IS NOT NULL AND TC2.THER_DISC_ID IN (13, 5, 8, 49) THEN TC2.EV_THERAPIST_ID
            ELSE NULL
        END
    ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC
) MostFrequentTherapist
CROSS APPLY (
    -- Subquery to find the most recent event for the student
    SELECT TOP 1 
        TC3.SCH_Name
    FROM #TherapistCred TC3
    WHERE TC3.ATT_STUDENT_ID = TC.ATT_STUDENT_ID
      AND TC3.THER_SER = TC.THER_SER
      AND TC3.IEP_IEP_ID = TC.IEP_IEP_ID
      AND (
          (TC3.ESO_SIGNER_ID IS NOT NULL AND TC3.ESO_DISC_ID IN (13, 5, 8, 49))
          OR (TC3.ATT_Supervisor_ID IS NOT NULL AND TC3.ATT_DISC_ID IN (13, 5, 8, 49))
          OR (TC3.EV_THERAPIST_ID IS NOT NULL AND TC3.THER_DISC_ID IN (13, 5, 8, 49))
      )
    ORDER BY TC3.EV_EVENTEND DESC
) MostRecentEvent
ORDER BY TC.ATT_STUDENT_ID, TC.IEP_IEP_ID;

select distinct

SD.DIS_Name District_Name
,SD.School School_Name
,SD.ATT_STUDENT_ID Student_ID
,S.STU_FirstName Student_FirstName
,S.STU_LastName Student_LastName
,S.STU_DateOfBirth Student_DOB
,SD.IEP_IEP_ID IEP_ID
,SD.IEP_BeginningDate
,SD.IEP_EndingDate
,SD.IEP_Service_Type
,SD.Supervisor_Therapist_ID
,T.THE_FirstName Supervisor_FirstName
,T.THE_LastName Supervisor_LastName
,D.DISC_Abbrev Supervisor_Cred
,T.THE_Email Supervisor_Email
,Case 
	When T.THE_STELLAR_EMPLOYEE = 1 
	Then 'Yes' 
	Else 'No' 
End as StellarTherapist

from #SupervisorData SD
join STUDENTS S
	on S.STU_STUDENT_ID = SD.ATT_STUDENT_ID
Join THERAPISTS T
	on T.THE_THERAPISTS_ID = SD.Supervisor_Therapist_ID
JOIN CREDHealthLicense THL
    ON THL.CREDHL_THERAPIST_ID = T.THE_THERAPISTS_ID
JOIN CREDLicenseStatus 
    ON CREDLicenseStatus_ID = THL.CREDHL_CREDSTAT_ID
    AND CREDLicenseStatus_ID NOT IN (2,4,5,6)
JOIN DISCIPLINES D
    ON DISC_Discipline_ID = THL.CREDHL_LICTYPE
    AND DISC_Discipline_ID IN (13, 5, 8, 49)
Where SD.SVA_SERVICES_ID IN (@Service)      
AND SD.DIS_DISTRICTS_ID IN (@District)    
--AND TC.EV_EVENTSTART BETWEEN @StartDate AND @EndDate  
AND T.THE_STELLAR_EMPLOYEE IN (@StellarTherapist)    

Order by SD.DIS_Name, SD.ATT_STUDENT_ID, SD.IEP_IEP_ID;

```

The first part of the query gets all of the therapist credentials by Events, it also pulls most of those student’s information into the first temp table. The second temp table ranks the therapist on who is the student’s supervisor for those events. Since there are Event Therapists, Supervising Therapists, and Therapists that sign off on events I had to determine which therapist needed to be assigned to that student. Each event is different when it comes to the therapist.

Actually it’s like two of the table names are reversed. The RESULTS table (“Level of Assistance” in the UI) contains things like “Independent”, “Supervision”, “Minimal Assist”, etc. The Level_of_Assistance table (“Results” in the UI) contains “0-10% Accuracy”, “10-20% Accuracy”, etc., as well as “Within Normal Limits” and “Not Within Normal Limits - see comments”. The labels in the UI appear to be right. The ACTIONS table contains things like “demonstrated”, “educated”, “facilitated”. It’s labeled “Supports” in the UI. I could see a case for using either name.

I mentioned yesterday about not being able to delete intervention types that have been used in an event. That’s because there’s a foreign key relationship from INTERVENTIONS (the reference table) to EVENT_INTERVENTIONS (basically, the repeater on the Therapy screen, which contains those four data elements). INTERVENTIONS has a column with the service ID, so each intervention type record can only be used for a single service (“other - see comments” is repeated for each service).

The other three are a little more complicated. There’s a ServiceResult table that ties RESULTS records to service IDs, a ServiceLevelOfAssistance table that ties Level_of_Assistance records  to service IDs, and a ServiceActions table that ties ACTIONS records to service IDs. We use those tables to constrain the choices that are displayed in the UI. There’s not actually a foreign key relationship, though (it would have been hard to do that under the circumstances), so there’s nothing at the database that limits those fields on EVENT_INTERVENTIONS to only the defined values. I mention that just to say that we’ll need to be a little more careful with those, because the database would let us delete them without complaining.

content.S:
I wanted to also do kind of a “postmortem” on the project, to document some of the unexpected problems and maybe some lessons learned.

The first delay was all on my side. I had the idea of using a tool called Terraform to create and manage the AWS resources. I had used Terraform with good results before, but what I was trying to do here was a little more detailed, and some things didn’t work the way I expected. The biggest thing was AWS System Manager, which runs automated processes on AWS nodes. The idea was to set up a System Manager job that we could trigger anytime we made a change to the code, and automatically update the test system. But it just wouldn’t work, no matter what I tried. So I had to shift my approach to be just a little more manual, but in the end, it was still 98% automated, and the remaining 2% only took a minute or so. It really wasn’t worth the time I spent trying to get to 100%. So that part was annoying, but had nothing to do with Stellar Docs, really.

The next big hangup was with managing the JavaScript scripts that Stellar Docs uses for client-side interactivity. We’re using the jQuery library, which was so widespread back in its day that it will probably never fully go away. But the versions we’re using are very old. We use version 1.3.2 (2009) in some places and 1.7.2 (2011) in others. I tried to update to the latest stable version, 3.7 (2023), but that version wasn’t compatible with the version of jQuery UI, 1.7.1 (2009), that we use for the datepicker control. At some point, we should probably find a compatible combination, or choose a different datepicker. Having such an old version of jQuery is a security risk.

Once I decided to fall back to the current versions of jQuery, the next issue was with how those scripts are bundled for download to the client. The bundling mechanism that the application was built with isn’t supported by the current version of Visual Studio, even for backward-compatible ASP.NET 4.8 projects, which is the last “framework” version of .NET. I would have had to change too many places to use the newer mechanism, so I decided just to include the script references directly on the page. There’s no big downside to doing it that way, it’s just a little more code.

I finally got through all those issues, and thought I was home free, but then I hit a major snag with the precompilation step of the publish process.

ASP.NET Web Forms supported two different models: Web Site Project (WSP) and Web Application Project (WAP). WSPs were nice for mostly static sites that maybe just needed a little bit of automation here or there. Their compile-on-demand model was perfectly fine for that type of content. For data-driven or highly interactive applications, WAPs offered a better developer experience because they could be compiled before deployment, making the IDE tooling work better, and providing much better confidence in your changes. I’m sure there was a good reason for creating Stellar Docs as a WSP, but ultimately it has made it harder to get it working anywhere except the Stellar server.

You can’t really convert a WSP directly to a WAP. The best option is to create a new WAP and gradually files over. That’s what I did, but I kept running into all kinds of conflicts during precompilation. I was able to work through them gradually, but it was a painful process of untangling dependencies.

Exception handling was another issue I ran into. On the one hand, having the exceptionLogger table, and a global default error handler that logs the exception details to that table, is a huge help. The problem is with how we use that feature. In some places, it’s fine. The operation fails, the error is logged, and the application continues to function. In other cases, the error is logged, but it leaves the application in a weird state that it can’t recover from, and there’s no choice but to reboot it. 

In the worst-case scenario, which I saw several times, errors are caught and the quietly swallowed. That happens a couple of different ways. One is in the application code, in the form of a `try...catch` block where the `catch` section is empty. That explicitly tells the application to ignore any errors in the `try` section and bypass the global error handling. The other big case is in stored procedures. I saw several where a complex transaction was wrapped in a `try...catch`, and the `catch` rolled back the transaction as it should, but then basically just returned a “didn’t work” response to the application, without any details. Those were really hard to troubleshoot because I had to recreate the state of the application at the time of the stored procedure call, and then call the procedure step by step until I saw where it failed.

There’s also a lot of complicated JavaScript stuff that happens entirely outside the application handling. That caused me a few headaches as well.

The last big area of problems was with how we connect to the database. There are several different models in use:

- via library classes in StellarLibraryCS, most of which use stored procedures
- stored procedures called directly from the code
- parameterized SQL statements called directly from the code
- concatenated SQL statements called directly from the code
- a handful of Entity Framework calls

There are a number of subvarieties within those models, and a number of cases where the models aren’t implemented correctly, or, candidly, aren’t doing what the programmer apparently thought they were doing. Having that many different ways of accessing the data isn’t a *problem* per se, but it definitely makes the code base harder to work with.

A related issue is the sheer number of stored procedures. I’m quite sure not all of them are used, but I was surprised at how many actually were. Some of the operations within Stellar Docs require a long series of stored procedure calls. It makes it hard to troubleshoot, but it also leads to kind of a “worst of both worlds” situation where you’ve got the added complexity of managing stored procedures outside the main application code, but not really getting the full benefits of using them.

One last little quirk that slowed me down in numerous small ways was the extent of “dead code” in the code base. Some it was commented out, but a lot of it was just sort of left in there. Probably whatever used to call it got removed. It doesn’t hurt anything as far as the execution of the program (it’s probably not even included in the final compiled version) but it sure gets in the way when you’re trying to troubleshoot.

To be clear this is not an “everything is terrible” kind of rant. Stellar Docs has kept on humming for all these years. It *works* fine, it’s just a little hard to work on. And since I spent so much time on this fix, I thought it would be a shame not to capture any kind of lessons learned and maybe some action items that could improve things.

Long-term, I do think it’s probably worthwhile to consider moving off ASP.NET Web Forms to a more modern platform. It’s not just that Web Forms is *old*—plenty of old stuff still works fine, and Web Forms will likely continue to work fine for years to come—but  the underlying development paradigm ended up ultimately being rejected by the development community (and Microsoft itself). If it were a Java or PHP application from that era, I would say keep it running. Or a Microsoft ASP.NET MVC application from the early 2010s, same thing. But Web Forms was an evolutionary dead end. You’ll have a harder and harder time finding people to work on it, and tools that support it.

In the shorter term, here are some recommendations to consider:

**Migrate to an ASP.NET Web Forms WAP**

I’ve already done probably 60-70% of the work for that. It would make everything else you do a lot easier, safer, and more predictable.

**Upgrade to the latest version of jQuery**

jQuery was *so* ubiquitous back in the day, that there are undoubtedly plenty of exploits that target it. Using such an old version is a real risk. Changing to a newer version may require some other changes, including different UI controls, but it may also give us a good chance to hack away at some of the unused code.

**Standardize the data access model**

This is not as hard as it sounds. I basically did it for the therapy screen as part of my fix. Essentially, you choose a model and then make a whole lot of little, mostly very simple, changes to make everything use that model. Considering the current situation, my recommendation would actually be to *mostly* switch to parameterized SQL queries, retaining the more complex stored procedures. 

Parameterized SQL is a lot like stored procedures—same security benefits, for all practical purposes the same performance benefits—but your data logic is all located within (or very close to) your application code. While we’re doing this, we could also combine some of those multi-step stored procedure sequences into either parameterized SQL statements or stored procedures, whichever made the most sense.

**Sanitize the code base for dead code, bad error handling, and other weirdness**

Not a wholesale rewrite, but selectively and progressively identifying and correcting any of these situations that made the troubleshooting difficult.

I've been doing some research on using Elixir and Phoenix. 

## Summary of Claude conversation (by Claude):

Evaluated Elixir/Phoenix/LiveView as an alternative to Go/React for a quality management system targeting small-to-mid manufacturers. Initial concern was that Elixir's small community and hiring pool made it risky, but since this is a solo open-source side project, those concerns are largely moot. The real-time, fault-tolerance, and data integrity requirements of the QMS are actually a strong fit for Elixir/OTP—better in some ways than Go. Phoenix/LiveView reduces frontend complexity compared to a React SPA, and the idiomatic approach would be a modular monolith with Elixir contexts (configuration, event intake, reporting/subscriptions) rather than microservices—simpler to operate and a better fit than a polyglot Go+Phoenix architecture connected via gRPC. Ecto (Postgres, obviously) is a good fit given a preference for explicit, non-magical data handling. Library ecosystem is thinner than Go's but adequate for this use case; PDF/reporting is the one area to watch, with a carve-out to a separate component as a fallback. IDE support (VS Code + ElixirLS) is functional but not first-class. Phoenix LiveDashboard provides strong out-of-the-box observability. Deploys as a standard Linux binary, containerizes cleanly for K8s or Fly.io.
The main risk isn't the technology—it's maintaining momentum on a project with a history of being deprioritized when client work arrives. Scheduled dedicated time has been identified as the key process change to address that.

## Summary of Gemini conversation about Postgres (by Gemini):

To wrap this up for your future self: we successfully moved your Phoenix development environment from a "serverless" cloud (Supabase) back to your repurposed Ubuntu laptop (192.168.1.155) to avoid IPv6 networking headaches and potential usage costs. The setup now bypasses the complex SSL and pooling requirements of managed hosts, opting for a high-performance local TCP connection that provides lower latency and full control over your hardware.

Technically, the "magic" was in configuring Postgres to listen beyond localhost (listen_addresses = '*') and whitelisting your dev machine’s IP in pg_hba.conf. On the Phoenix side, we configured dev.exs and .env to target the laptop via its internal IP on port 5432, ensuring the Postgrex driver is forced to IPv4 (socket_options: [:inet]). Your project is now verified, connected, and ready for mix ecto.migrate.

## Summary of Gemini conversation about Elixir and Phoenix (by Gemini):

Project Architecture: The "Modular Monolith" (Go + Elixir)
The Stack: We are utilizing a "Best of Both Worlds" approach by pairing a Go-based Event Engine with an Elixir/Phoenix Dashboard, connected via gRPC.

Go (The Engine): Handles the "Industrial" heavy lifting—ingesting high-frequency sensor data, managing low-level hardware communication, and enforcing strict data types. It serves as the single source of truth for the system's state.

Elixir/Phoenix (The Dashboard): Acts as the "Air Traffic Controller." By using Phoenix LiveView, we move the UI state to the server, eliminating the need for a complex React/Redux frontend. This allows for real-time, "socket-first" updates (like defect alerts) with minimal code.

Postgres (The Memory): A unified database that stores both the raw event logs from the Go engine and the relational user/account data from Phoenix.

The Philosophy:
This architecture is optimized for a solo developer building a mission-critical product. It prioritizes uptime through Erlang’s "self-healing" process model and speed of delivery by leveraging Phoenix’s built-in tools (like phx.gen.auth for industrial PIN/Azure AD login). We are trading the "statelessness" of REST for a persistent, stateful connection that survives flaky factory Wi-Fi and provides a superior developer experience without the "JavaScript fatigue."

---

Actually I haven't completely decided about whether to use Phoenix at all, and if so, whether to use it for the whole thing in a modular monolith (there are compelling reasons) or only for the UI and then have Go micro services.

content.S:
***Initial notes***



Review error logs for frequent errors and warnings, fix those
Apply static analysis tools to code base, address any issues
Use performance profiling tools to identify and address any performance bottlenecks or memory usage issues
Add automated unit tests
Graceful degradation - keep core functions accessible
Ability to run app from a single working server

Document troubleshooting steps for frequent problems

## Review error logs to identify and address frequent errors and warnings

### Why Recommended
Errors and warnings in the application logs indicate an unexpected condition that could be causing a poor user experience or possibly affecting application security, stability, or performance
### Detailed Steps
Review available application logs, scanning for ERR and WRN entries
For each entry, determine the cause of the error or warning
Triage the errors and warnings according to:
 - impact on information security
 - impact on application stability
 - impact on user experience and productivity
 Identify options for addressing the error or warning
 Address any where the cost to fix is clearly less than the impact
 If the issue is nontrivial and the fix might impact users or overall system functionality, consult with Tex Tech
### Success Metrics
#### Baseline
number of errors and warnings logged per day over 7-day period
#### Expected
100% reduction in errors and at least 85% reduction in warnings vs baseline

## Apply static analysis and performance profiling tools

### Why Recommended
Languages, runtimes, and profiling tools have improved significantly since 2017. Static analysis tools can recommend code changes to make use of these improvements. Performance profiling tools can locate "hot paths" in application resource usage to guide performance optimizations and can point out problematic memory usage.
### Detailed Steps
Use JetBrains Rider to review suggested code actions
Apply trivial fixes, make note of more significant recommendations
Use JetBrains dotTrace to collect detailed performance metrics
Use JetBrains dotMemory to identify any memory usage issues
Create a prioritized list of improvements
Implement the most impactful improvements
Perform the analysis again after each significant improvement
### Success Metrics
#### Baseline
Performance metrics (e.g., average request latency for key API endpoints, CPU/memory usage during peak load for Legacy) as measured by dotTrace and dotMemory before implementing any optimizations.
#### Expected
 - A measurable improvement (e.g., 5-10%) in the performance of at least one identified "hot path" in the application, as indicated by reduced execution time in dotTrace.
 - A noticeable reduction in memory allocations or improved memory utilization in a specific area of concern identified by dotMemory (if any such areas are found).
 - Implementation of all "trivial" code fixes suggested by Rider.
 - Documentation of any significant code improvement recommendations from Rider that require more substantial effort for potential implementation in future cycles.

## Improve "failure mode" functionality
### Why Recommended
TTDS is generally stable, but there have been instances where the entire application became unresponsive due to either an application-related problem or an environmental problem that could been isolated to a specific section of the application.
### Detailed Steps
List all significant functional paths through the application
Identify functional paths most critical to Tex Tech operations
List external services on which the application depends (power, Internet, network, domain, database, etc.)
Map dependencies within application
For each functional path, determine which services and application dependencies the functional path requires (its "demands")
For each demand, determine whether:
- there is no reasonable functional mode in the absence of that demand
- an alternative could be substituted for that demand, perhaps with limited features or performance
- an explicit redundancy should be implemented
### Success Metrics
All functional paths and associated demands documented
Top 10 critical paths demonstrated to be as resilient as feasible given physical plant constraints
## Add automated unit tests
### Why Recommended
Automated unit tests run within the code base and can be highly effective at ensuring that changes and enhancements (1) work fully as intended and (2) don't break any existing functionality. They serve as helpful documentation of how the code is intended to work. In the long term, they tend to shorten development time because they reduce the amount of debugging and testing issues. The current code base has a limited number of these tests but could be significantly improved.
### Detailed Steps
Use JetBrains dotCover to determine the test coverage percentage for the .NET components
Use JetBrains WebStorm to determine the test coverage percentage for the Web front-end
Add unit tests as needed, prioritizing more business-critical sections of the code and those with complex business or UI logic
Incorporate automated testing into the build pipelines
### Success Metrics
#### Baseline
current test coverage
#### Expected
Test coverage at least 70%, with non-covered sections justified
Automated unit tests are run as part of the build pipeline; all tests must pass before a build can be released

## Improve monitoring and telemetry
### Why Recommended
Currently, the first indication of a problem is usually application slowness or unavailability. Rebooting the servers often resolves the problem, but causes downtime and potential data loss. When rebooting doesn't solve the problem, engaging development can be time-consuming and clunky, relying on passing text-based log files via online file shares or email. More advanced monitoring and telemetry can make it easier to identify problems that have cause—or might soon cause—a loss of service.
### Detailed Steps
Standardize logging
Evaluate shipping logs to S3
Incorporate OpenTelemetry into .NET applications
Identify and implement a monitoring solution
Add a '/health' endpoint to each service
Figure out a telemetry collection and alerting strategy (something with OpenTelemetryCollector?)

NinjaOne? (tickets or health updates)
### Success Metrics

## Document support details
### Why Recommended
Tex Tech's daily operations rely heavily on TTDS, yet the core support team for the application is a single internal IT analyst and a single external developer. If the application should experience an outage and either or both of these individuals were unavailable for an extended time, the business impact could potentially be serious. It would be beneficial to document application components, features, possible points of failure, and troubleshooting steps so that other internal Tex Tech personnel could do first-line support. In the unlikely event that the developer was no longer available, this documentation, along with the source code, would enable a new developer to take over application support.
### Detailed Steps
Create a high-level architecture diagram, showing all core components and their interactions and dependencies
Create more detailed component, process flow, state transition, and sequence diagrams to document critical functions
Create a list of likely failure points and steps to troubleshoot them
### Success Metrics
Tex Tech technical personnel unfamiliar with TTDS review and approve the documentation

## Modernize and streamline sections of the application that make intensive use of the jQuery library
### Why Recommended
When HighlandReporting was created in 2017, the state of the art for .NET development was ASP.NET MVC using Razor pages for server-side text templating and jQuery for enhanced client-side interactivity. jQuery has been largely superseded by improvements to the JavaScript language and by improved client-side tools such as React. jQuery is still fully functional and will remain so, but newer developers will be less likely to be familiar with it. Also, the newer tools are generally much faster to work with and are better at managing complex application behavior.
### Detailed Steps
Identify the application features that could most benefit from modernization
Develop functional front-end tests using Selenium or similar tooling to ensure baseline functionality for those features
Confirm with Tex Tech that no changes are desired for those features; if changes are desired, adjust the tests to reflect those changes
Migrate the identified features either to React if practical, or to a more modern module-based JavaScript paradigm if moving to React would be too initially complex
Run the tests to ensure 100% behavioral parity
### Success Metrics
Top 5 features are migrated to a newer JavaScript tool set

A "quality event" is an abstract term that can include the following:
- measurement of a specific aspect of the subject (thickness, thread count, width, etc.)
- the result of a laboratory test against the subject (strength, flammability, permeability, etc.)
- a defect identified as part of a visual inspection

Quality events occur as part of a predefined quality management activity. That activity can optionally be associated with a predefined set of measurements and tests.

Quality events are registered against a "subject", which can be:
- a specific item being manufactured
- a sample derived from a lot, as in a continuous manufacturing process 

Each subject has its own unique identifier
